hook.line: After ten messages about times and places, someone has to close the deal. In Colombia that someone starts with *entonces*.
hook.en: So we're meeting on Saturday, right?

examples.en: So we're meeting on Saturday, right?

examples.es: Entonces nos vemos a las ocho en el café.
examples.en: So we'll see each other at eight at the café.
So, are you coming or not? (to a friend)

examples.es: Tengo mucho trabajo, o sea que no puedo salir.
examples.en: I've got loads of work, so I can't go out.

examples.es: Vale está en Medellín, o sea que no viene el viernes.
examples.en: Vale is in Medellín, so she's not coming on Friday.

examples.es: O sea que no tienes boleta.
examples.en: So you don't have a ticket. (to a friend)

rule:
Two ways to say so.

*Entonces* opens a sentence to sum up or confirm a plan, often with *¿no?* at the end: *Entonces quedamos el sábado, ¿no?* On its own, *¿Entonces qué?* means so, what's the plan?

*O sea que* comes after what was just said and draws the conclusion from it: *Tengo trabajo, o sea que no puedo.* It also works on what someone else said, often with a little surprise: *O sea que no vienes.*

You already know *así que*: same idea. The verbs after all three stay normal.

One trap: in the middle of a story, *entonces* sounds like so, as if one thing caused the next. For plain and then, use *y después*.
smallPrint: Teachers call these consecutive connectors: words that introduce a result.

options: So we're meeting on Saturday, right?

readAndPick.es: No tengo plata, o sea que no voy.
options: I'm not going because I have no money.
I have no money, so I'm not going.

readAndPick.es: No voy porque no tengo plata.
options: I'm not going because I have no money.
I have no money, so I'm not going.
So, are you coming or not?

readAndPick.es: Mariana tiene una cita, o sea que no viene.
options: Mariana has a date because she isn't coming.
Mariana has a date, so she isn't coming.
If Mariana has a date, she isn't coming.

readAndPick.es: Comimos y después fuimos a bailar.
options: We ate, so we went dancing.
We ate and then went dancing.
So, what's the plan? Are we going to the concert?
Why not? Shall we go to the concert?

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *entonces* or *porque* and type the whole sentence: ___ quedamos el sábado, ¿no? (So we're meeting on Saturday, right?)
yourTurn.why: To sum up and confirm a plan, start with *entonces*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *o sea que* or *porque* and type the whole sentence: Tengo mucho trabajo, ___ no puedo salir. (I've got loads of work, so I can't go out.)
yourTurn.answer: Tengo mucho trabajo, o sea que no puedo salir.
yourTurn.why: The result comes second, so *o sea que*. *Porque* would make the work the result.

yourTurn.prompt: Confirm the plan with a friend: So we'll see each other at eight at the café.
yourTurn.answer: Entonces nos vemos a las ocho en el café.
accept: Entonces nos vemos en el café a las ocho.
Entonces nos vemos a las ocho en el café, ¿no?
yourTurn.why: *Entonces* at the start wraps up the plan.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: So, are you coming or not?
yourTurn.why: *Entonces* in front asks for a final answer.

yourTurn.prompt: A friend says he has no ticket. Draw the conclusion: So you're not coming.
yourTurn.why: *O sea que* draws the conclusion from what someone just told you.

yourTurn.prompt: Flip it round with *o sea que*: *No puedo salir porque tengo mucho trabajo.*
yourTurn.answer: Tengo mucho trabajo, o sea que no puedo salir.
accept: Tengo mucho trabajo, entonces no puedo salir.
Tengo mucho trabajo, así que no puedo salir.
yourTurn.why: *Porque* gives the reason; *o sea que* puts the reason first and the result second.

pitfalls.right: Comimos y después fuimos a bailar.
pitfalls.why: Careful. *Entonces* here sounds like the eating caused the dancing. For one thing after another, say *y después*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tengo mucho trabajo, porque no puedo salir.
pitfalls.right: Tengo mucho trabajo, o sea que no puedo salir.
pitfalls.why: *Porque* gives a reason, not a result. After the reason, the result needs *o sea que*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tengo mucho trabajo, tan no puedo salir.
pitfalls.right: Tengo mucho trabajo, o sea que no puedo salir.
pitfalls.why: English so has two jobs. *Tan* is only for so tired, so big. For so as a result, use *o sea que* or *así que*.

personal: Close a real plan you have this week, the Colombian way: *Entonces...*, *¿no?*
